Installations Page
Developer tools CMS 2025

Installations
Page

Designed and shipped installation analytics that gave developers site-level visibility into how their apps were used.

Overview

TL;DR

  • I designed a page that developers needed: they had no way to see who installed their apps, so they emailed support for basic usage data.
  • I mapped the gap with the PM, worked through permission levels and PII limits with engineering, and shipped part of it in code.
  • Developers who found it used it, and the feedback has been positive.
Background

The problem

Developers had no visibility into who was installing their apps. It came up in almost every developer interview. They were building workarounds and emailing our support team just to get basic usage data. Customers who contacted them for support often didn't know their site URL or instance ID, so developers kept their own installation records.

They needed it for:

  • Monitor the app's growth: check install dates to spot patterns and measure marketing
  • Support users by instance ID: find their email and site URL to give targeted support
  • Understand the audience: filter by plan, and see who canceled or uninstalled
Approach

Research

The PM and I started by mapping the gap, and user interviews confirmed it was a top pain point.

  • Developers needed this data for user support, marketing, and trends
  • Almost every developer interview raised it
  • Developers asked to see installations in an interface, get them by email, and receive them through webhooks, mostly for security, customer support, and marketing
  • I looked at how Shopify and Apple's App Store Connect handle the same problem for their ecosystems

Approach

Design principles

Four principles came out of the research and the constraints.

Explain, don't hide.

When data is restricted or missing, a tooltip says why and how to get access.

Start from what developers asked for.

The default view comes from the interviews and requests.

Legal sets the boundaries.

PII and legal rules decided what could be shown, and to whom, before any layout.

Let developers shape the view.

Filters, column customization, and export.

Approach

Challenges

  • Personal and business emails needed different permission levels, so not every developer could see every field.
  • The backend APIs decided which fields we could show, and when. Some fields can come back empty.
  • Some of the data coming back from the server was incorrect, and I caught it during implementation.
  • The migration was complex enough that we launched with a small controlled rollout.
  • We wanted to connect the installations list to Wix's contacts product, so developers could filter their users, email them, and set up automations. A technical gap between site-level and account-level data blocked it.
Server: mapping out why some fields return empty
Solution

Design

  • Started with a quick mock in Figma Make to validate the direction with stakeholders and users
  • Designed the page layout, filters, data export, and column customization in Figma
  • Defined the default view with the user interviews and requests in mind
  • Handled missing data with contextual tooltips explaining why some data is missing, for example when the user didn't fill out their business name
Figma MakeInitial exploration.

Delivery

Delivery

  • Joined the implementation team, using Cursor and Claude Code to add features and fix bugs
  • Contributed a year selector to the Wix Design System in code, making it available across the platform
  • Caught major server-side bugs where the data coming back was incorrect
  • Led UX writing for the project, including the feature's documentation, working closely with technical writers
  • Launched with a small controlled rollout given the migration complexity. It's live now
CursorFeatures added and bugs fixed during implementation.
Results

Results & impact

Since opening to all developers, the majority of those who visited the Wix Developer Center and had published apps discovered the page. Of those who saw it, the majority took action, copying data, opening sites, and applying filters. This was after a quiet launch with no promotion.

What developers said:

  • "We already had email sequences hooked on webhooks, but this lets us manually follow up with users, especially for the non-technical team members."
  • "Very good feature overall, thank you!"
Next steps

Next steps & bottom line

Next steps: The next step was views for the table, so developers can save how they look at their data. The roadmap also included cancellation reasons, deeper filtering, tags and notes for developers, revenue per user, and eventually connecting the page to the inbox and email marketing tools. Not enough developers were exposed to the feature, so making it easier to find was also planned.

Bottom line

The project started with a complaint that came up in almost every interview. My job was to decide which fields developers see and what the default view shows. Later on, I got to ship features myself using AI tools.
